Dattātreya Tantra
------------------------------------------
This is a minor work belonging to the Vāmācara group of तन्त्रस्.
It has 24 paṭalas or chapters and contains 395 verses.
The topics dealt with are as follows:
Māraṇa (getting an undesirable person or an enemy killed); mohana (deluding any person); stambhana (arresting the movement of any living being or stopping the working of any object like fire); vidveṣaṇa (bringing about enmity between persons previously well-disposed); उच्चाटन (driving away anyone from his place); sarvajanavaśīkaraṇa (controlling the minds of all persons); ākarṣana (attracting anyone towards oneself); इन्द्रजाल (several modes of magic); yakṣiṇīsādhanā (rites aimed at pleasing the 14 Yakṣiṇīs or minor goddesses); rasāyanaprayoga (science of converting base metals into gold or alchemy); kālajñāna (methods of knowing the exact time of one’s or others’ death); anāhāra-योग (specially prepared medicines that help in overcoming hunger and thirst); nidhidarśana (discovering hidden wealth through psychic insight); vandhyāputravatīkaraṇam (certain specially prepared potions by drinking which, a barren woman can conceive); mṛtavatsājīvana (helping a women who is losing children, to give birth to long living ones); jayasaṁvāda (rite that helps one to win in debates); vājīkaraṇa (means of increasing virility); bhūtagrahādinivāraṇa (driving away the evil spirits).
The text gives the mantras needed for each of the rites and all the other instructions necessary.
Readers of such texts are warned not to practise any of the rites without the guidance of the experts.

Dattātreya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad belonging to the cult of विष्णु and classed among the ones of the Atharvaṇaveda. There are three khaṇḍas or sections and a total of nine long mantras, all in prose, except one.
The four-faced ब्रह्मा once approached नारायण, the Supreme Lord of the universe in the Satyakṣetra—the region situated between the rivers गङ्गा and Yamunā—and requested him to teach that transcendental wisdom by which one can become free from the rounds of birth and death. नारायण advised him to meditate upon his Abode of pure सत्त्व (the quality of substance of purity and effulgence). Those who meditate thus and realise that the Lord is ‘Datta,’ since he gives (datta = what is granted or given) the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्, and also declare it to others, will never again be bound in सṁसार or transmigratory existence.
Having been instructed by नारायण thus, ब्रह्मा meditated upon the दत्तात्रेय aspect of नारायण and taught it as Sat (the eternal Truth) to others.
Next, a series of mantras of दत्तात्रेय are given, classifying them as ekākṣara (one-lettered), ṣaḍakṣara (six lettered) and so on.
They are:
(1) dām ॥
(2) Oṁ śrīṁ ह्रीṁ klīṁ glauṁ drām ॥
(3) drāṁ dattātreyāya namaḥ ॥
(4) Om āṁ ह्रीṁ krom ehi दत्तात्रेय स्वाहा ॥
(5) Om aiṁ kroṁ klīṁ klūṁ hrāṁ
hrīṁ hrūṁ sauḥ dattātreyāya स्वाहा ॥
(6) दत्तात्रेय hare kṛṣṇa
unmattānandadāyaka ।
digambara mune bāla पिशाच jñānasāgara ॥
The next section gives a very long मन्त्र, called ‘mālāmantra’. It begins thus: ‘Oṁ namo bhagavate dattātreyāya smaraṇamātra-santuṣṭaya....’ and so on. It ends with the words, ‘Oṁ namaśśivāya ityupaniṣat.’
The third or the last section delineates the fruits of the practice of this esoteric science. The results he will get will be equal to that got by repeating the Gāyatrīmantra one lakh times or the Mahārudramantra one lakh times and so on. He purifies a hundred of his predecessors and a hundred of his descendants. He is never tainted even by the most heinous of sins like killing a cow. The knowledge of all mantras and yogas accrue to him of their own accord. In other words he becomes a jīvanmukta, one liberated even while living.
See also DATTĀTREYA and UPANIṢADS.

dattaka
(‘[a son] given to oneself [by others]’)
------------------------------------------
The ancient sages of India gave as much importance to life in the next world (pitṛloka, the world of manes) as to the life here. Hence they always hankered after an aurasaputra or a son born out of the wife married as per the rules given in the धर्मशास्त्रस्. It was this son (or sons) who had the right to the property of his ड़थेर् and also perform the śrāddha ceremony after his death. (See ŚRĀDDHA.)
If a person had no children from his wife, he was permitted to adopt a son who was called ‘dattaka.’ In course of time elaborate rules were framed for the process of अदोप्तिओन्.
Every male Hindu who is a major and of a sound मिन्द् can adopt a son, if he himself has no son or grandson or near (male) relative, who is eligible to perform the śrāddha after his death. The boy to be adopted must be from the same caste.
The primary right to give a son for अदोप्तिओन् rests with the natural ड़थेर्. The मोथेर् can also do so provided she gets the consent of her husband or is a widow.
Persons having more than one son only can give a son for अदोप्तिओन् by others. They should not, however give the eldest son.
If there is only one son, he should not be given away in अदोप्तिओन्. However, even this has been sometimes allowed on the condition that the boy should be considered as the son of both the natural ड़थेर् and adopting ड़थेर्. In such cases, the adopted boy is called ‘dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa’.
The procedure of अदोप्तिओन् given in the धर्मशास्त्रस् has several steps. The more important ones are: ड़स्तिन्ग् by the adopter the previous day, offering मधुपर्क (See MADHUPARKA for details.) to the officiating priest, performance of the dattahoma using Ṛgvedic verses, holding both hands of the boy symbolic of receiving him into ones own family and offering of boiled rice.
By such an अदोप्तिओन्, the boy now becomes like an aurasaputra or natural son, enjoying all the rights and privileges and also bound to discharge all the duties and responsibilities.
If a natural son is born to the adopter later on, then the दत्तक gets only one-fourth share in the property.
Though अदोप्तिओन् was confined mostly to boys, girls too could be adopted. The two famous examples in our epics are those of Śāntā the adopted daughter of रोमपाद and कुन्ती, of Kuntibhoja.

Dattātreya
(‘One [who was] given to अत्रि’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य् abounds in stories of Lord विष्णु’s avatāras or incarnations which may be pūrṇāvatāras (full manifestations) like श्रीकृष्ण or aṁśāvatāras (partial manifestations) like कपिल or even āveśāvatāras (temporary infilling of the divine power) like परशुराम. दत्तात्रेय is regarded as an अṁशावतार.
He was the son of the sage अत्रि and अनसूया, one of the paragons of wifely virtues and chastity in the mythological lore. According to one of the accounts, अत्रि who was childless, performed severe austerities to please God and obtain a worthy son. All the three deities of the Hindu Trinity—Brahmā, विष्णु and Śiva—appeared before him and granted his desire by being born through their aspects, as three sons: ब्रह्मा as चन्द्र, विष्णु as Datta and शिव as Dūrvāsas.
According to another version, the three who came to test the chastity of अनसूया were transformed into a child with three heads and six arms! This is how दत्तात्रेय was born.
Dattātreya also called ‘Datta’—has been described as a great sage, counted among the सप्तर्षिस् or seven sages in the Svārociṣa-मन्वन्तर. (See MANVANTARAS.) He was the originator of certain magical rites and the creator of the सोम plant. Sometimes pictured as a teacher of non-Āryan races he has been described as ritually impure. However, his powers of knowledge and enlightenment are so great that no impurity can ever taint him.
The great king Kārttavīryārjuna was a disciple of his.
A cult designated as the Datta-सम्प्रदाय has grown round him. It still prevails in Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Nepal. His temples are generally called ‘Dattamandira’ and it is his wooden sandals that are normally installed and worshipped. His temples are at Māhūr (Maharashtra) Gāṇagāpura (Karnataka) and Wāḍi (Maharashtra). There is an old shrine on one of the peaks of the Girnar Hill in Gujarat.
The sect of the Mahānubhāvas, started by चक्रधर (A.

) in Maharashtra considers दत्तात्रेय as a perfect manifestation of the Godhead.
Iconographically दत्तात्रेय may be shown with three heads and six hands, holding the emblems of ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव such as कमण्डलु (water pot), शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus) and त्रिशूल (trident). A bull (vṛṣabha, representing धर्म or righteousness) is shown as his mount. Sometimes, four dogs (representing the four वेदस्) are also shown as his constant companions.
The well-known treatise of Advaita Vedānta, the Avadhūtagītā, has been attributed to his authorship.
The दत्तात्रेय concept may be an attempt at harmonising the three cults of ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव. It may also have been the medium through which non-Vedic cults were brought into the Hindu fold.
